Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. So, I came in because... well, it's kind of hard to explain, but I've been having this issue with eating that's really starting to freak me out. I work at an entertainment complex—managing the floor, dealing with crowds, making sure the games and attractions are running smoothly—and my shifts usually go pretty late into the night. I'll sit down with a full takeout meal—like a massive double burger, large fries, maybe some nuggets—and I'll finish all of it. But then I just... I keep going. It's like a switch flips in my head. I'll head straight to the pantry and start tearing into bags of chips, cookies, sweets, honestly just whatever is sitting around in the apartment.

And then, maybe an hour or two later, I sort of snap out of it and look down at the coffee table, and I see all the empty takeout containers and the crushed chip bags, and I am just... I'm shocked. Like, genuinely, physically shocked by how much I just ate. It's just this massive mountain of food for one person, and I don't understand how I'm putting it all away, but it keeps happening after these late shifts, and I just can't seem to stop myself once I start.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Guilty? Um... I don't know if guilt is really the right word for it. I mean, I guess people usually feel bad about eating a bunch of junk food, but for me, it's not like I'm sitting there beating myself up or thinking, "Oh, you're a terrible person for eating all this." It's honestly more just... pure confusion. Like, absolute bewilderment. 

Like I was saying, I'll look down at the coffee table—it's this glass-top table I have right in front of my couch, this big brown leather sectional that is incredibly comfortable, which is probably part of the problem because once I sink into it after walking the arcade and laser tag floors all night, my legs are just done and I don't want to get back up. But I'll be sitting there, and my stomach will feel so incredibly stretched out and heavy, just this really uncomfortable, tight physical sensation, you know? And I'll look at the grease stains on the cardboard takeout boxes, and the empty sleeves of cookies—usually I go for those chocolate chip ones with the soft centers, or sometimes the peanut butter wafers—and I just stare at it all and think, "How did that even physically fit inside my stomach?" 

So it's not really guilt, if that makes sense. I'm not crying over it or feeling ashamed of myself in that moment. I just don't understand the mechanics of it. I'll usually just gather it all up in a big plastic garbage bag right then and there because I absolutely hate waking up to a messy living room. Since my shifts usually start later in the day, around 2 or 3 PM, I have all morning to just sit around my apartment, and I don't want to be staring at a pile of wrappers while I'm drinking my morning coffee. Control? Man, no. Not at all. That's actually the part that really messes with my head the most. Because, you know, at work, I'm totally in control. I have to be. I've got, you know, hundreds of kids and teenagers running around the arcade, the laser tag vests need to be charged, the prize counter has to be restocked, the ticket machines jam up, and I'm the one managing all of that. I'm thinking, "Okay, that's enough, you finished the takeout, you're full, just close the cookie sleeve. Roll the bag up and put a clip on it." I even have these heavy-duty plastic chip clips, the magnetic ones that stick to the fridge, they're right there in the drawer next to the sink, it would take two seconds to get up and use one. 

But my hands... it's like my hands don't even belong to my brain anymore. They just keep going. They just keep opening containers, ripping into the plastic wrappers, reaching back into the bags, over and over again until everything is gone. Every last crumb. And I'm just sitting there, completely disconnected from my own body, unable to stop my own hands from moving. It's so bizarre because I know I'm doing it, and I'm telling myself to stop, but the physical action just keeps happening anyway. So, yeah, any sense of control is just completely out the window once that switch flips.

I mean, I know people talk about "stress eating," like when you have a terrible day at work and you just want to eat a pint of ice cream to feel better. But for me, it's not like I'm sitting there feeling wound up or panicked while it's happening. 

Honestly, it's almost the opposite. Like I said, I'm usually coming off a ten-hour shift. By the time I get home, I am just completely physically exhausted. My feet ache, my back aches, my head is usually throbbing from all the flashing lights and the constant noise of the arcade machines and the music they play on a loop over the PA system—it's this playlist of top 40 hits that just repeats every three hours, and by the end of the week, I feel like I'm losing my mind listening to it. So when I finally get through the door of my apartment, drop my keys in the little ceramic bowl by the door, and kick my shoes off, I'm not feeling stressed. I'm just tired. 

And then, when the eating starts... like I was describing, it's just this weird, disconnected feeling. I'm not sitting there crying or worrying about my bills or stressing about work the next day. I'm just kind of... blank. It's like my brain just shuts off, or at least the part of my brain that feels emotions just goes offline for a bit. I'm just watching my hands move, watching myself eat all this food, and I'm not really feeling anything at all in the moment. It's just a mechanical process. Grab the food, open the wrapper, eat it, grab the next thing. So no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious or stressed during it. It's more like I'm just running on autopilot, completely numb to whatever else is going on in my head.

Like, absolute bewilderment. \n\nLike I was saying, I'll look down at the coffee table—it's this glass-top table I have right in front of my couch, this big brown leather sectional that is incredibly comfortable, which is probably part of the problem because once I sink into it after walking the arcade and laser tag floors all night, my legs are just done and I don't want to get back up. But I'll be sitting there, and my stomach will feel so incredibly stretched out and heavy, just this really uncomfortable, tight physical sensation, you know? And I'll look at the grease stains on the cardboard takeout boxes, and the empty sleeves of cookies—usually I go for those chocolate chip ones with the soft centers, or sometimes the peanut butter wafers—and I just stare at it all and think, \"How did that even physically fit inside my stomach?\" \n\nSo it's not really guilt, if that makes sense. I'm not crying over it or feeling ashamed of myself in that moment. I just don't understand the mechanics of it. I'll usually just gather it all up in a big plastic garbage bag right then and there because I absolutely hate waking up to a messy living room. Since my shifts usually start later in the day, around 2 or 3 PM, I have all morning to just sit around my apartment, and I don't want to be staring at a pile of wrappers while I'm drinking my morning coffee. So I'll haul it all out to the dumpster behind my building before I even go to bed. But yeah, to answer your question, I haven't really noticed feeling guilty about it. Just really, really baffled by the sheer volume of it all and how I didn't even realize I was doing it until it was over.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during these episodes after you get home from work?\n\nPatient: Control? Man, no. Not at all. That's actually the part that really messes with my head the most. Because, you know, at work, I'm totally in control. I have to be. I've got, you know, hundreds of kids and teenagers running around the arcade, the laser tag vests need to be charged, the prize counter has to be restocked, the ticket machines jam up, and I'm the one managing all of that. I'm the guy making the calls and keeping the chaos in check. But then I get home, and it's like... I don't even know. It's like I'm a completely different person. \n\nOnce I start eating on those nights, it’s honestly like I’m watching myself from the outside. Like I'm hovering somewhere up near the ceiling fan—which, by the way, I always keep on medium because my apartment gets incredibly stuffy at night, the ventilation in that building is just terrible—and I'm just looking down at myself on the couch. And in my head, my internal monologue is going a mile a minute. I'm literally telling myself to put the food away. I'm thinking, \"Okay, that's enough, you finished the takeout, you're full, just close the cookie sleeve. Roll the bag up and put a clip on it.\" I even have these heavy-duty plastic chip clips, the magnetic ones that stick to the fridge, they're right there in the drawer next to the sink, it would take two seconds to get up and use one. \n\nBut my hands... it's like my hands don't even belong to my brain anymore. They just keep going. They just keep opening containers, ripping into the plastic wrappers, reaching back into the bags, over and over again until everything is gone. Every last crumb. And I'm just sitting there, completely disconnected from my own body, unable to stop my own hands from moving. It's so bizarre because I know I'm doing it, and I'm telling myself to stop, but the physical action just keeps happening anyway. So, yeah, any sense of control is just completely out the window once that switch flips.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or stressed while you're eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: Anxious? Stressed? Uh... no, not really. It's not like that. I mean, I know people talk about \"stress eating,\" like when you have a terrible day at work and you just want to eat a pint of ice cream to feel better. But for me, it's not like I'm sitting there feeling wound up or panicked while it's happening. \n\nHonestly, it's almost the opposite. Like I said, I'm usually coming off a ten-hour shift. By the time I get home, I am just completely physically exhausted. My feet ache, my back aches, my head is usually throbbing from all the flashing lights and the constant noise of the arcade machines and the music they play on a loop over the PA system—it's this playlist of top 40 hits that just repeats every three hours, and by the end of the week, I feel like I'm losing my mind listening to it. So when I finally get through the door of my apartment, drop my keys in the little ceramic bowl by the door, and kick my shoes off, I'm not feeling stressed. I'm just tired. \n\nAnd then, when the eating starts... like I was describing, it's just this weird, disconnected feeling. I'm not sitting there crying or worrying about my bills or stressing about work the next day. I'm just kind of... blank. It's like my brain just shuts off, or at least the part of my brain that feels emotions just goes offline for a bit. I'm just watching my hands move, watching myself eat all this food, and I'm not really feeling anything at all in the moment. It's just a mechanical process. Grab the food, open the wrapper, eat it, grab the next thing. So no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious or stressed during it. It's more like I'm just running on autopilot, completely numb to whatever else is going on in my head.\n\n[Last Question]\nDo you ever make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?\n\n[Patient Info]\n- demographics: Male / 40 / entertainment_attendant_or_related_worker / associates\n- severity: Mild\n\n[Targeted Info]\nname: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging\nmanifestation: \"Sometimes after I get home and eat too much takeout or snacks, I go to the bathroom and make myself throw up so it won’t sit in me and turn into weight.\"\n\n[Conversation Style]\nYou are a Verbose patient.\nA verbose patient may\n1) provide excessively detailed responses when describing their symptoms and experiences, even when the details are directly relevant,\n2) elaborate extensively on the background, events, thoughts, feelings, and personal experiences surrounding their symptoms, and\n3) demonstrate difficulty allowing the doctor to guide the interview or move on to another clinical topic.\nThis is how you are, not a performance you put on in every reply — let it show as much or as little as the moment calls for.\n\nWhat to do:\n- Answer the doctor's last question with what [Targeted Info] holds, in your own words.\n- You are speaking out loud, not reading a line you prepared. Yeah, um... sometimes I do. It's just... well, because like I was saying before about how incredibly full and stretched out my stomach gets, it's just this heavy, rock-solid feeling. And I'll be sitting there on that leather sectional, and the apartment is totally quiet by that point except for the hum of the refrigerator—it's an older model, so the compressor is actually pretty loud when it kicks on in the middle of the night—and I just start thinking about all that food. All those empty takeout containers and the sleeves of snacks and whatever else I just ate. 

And I just... I can't stand the thought of it just sitting in there. You know? Like, my metabolism definitely isn't what it used to be now that I'm forty. I'm on my feet all day at the arcade, sure, but I just know that if I let all that grease and sugar just sit in my stomach overnight while I'm sleeping, it's going to absorb right into me and turn straight into weight. I can almost picture it happening, just sitting there digesting and turning into fat while I'm just lying in bed. 

So, yeah, sometimes after I get home and eat way too much of that takeout or all those snacks, I'll finally force myself up off the couch and go down the hall to the bathroom. It's a really narrow hallway, and the bathroom is right at the end, and the fluorescent light above the mirror in there is super bright, which is honestly awful at 3 AM when your eyes are already tired. But I'll go in there, and I'll lift the lid, and I'll just... make myself throw up. Just to get it out of me. Because if I can just empty it out and flush it away, then I don't have to worry about it sitting in me and turning into all this extra weight. It's just a way to kind of undo the physical damage of it all, I guess.

How often... well, if I really sit down and think about the timeline, it's been pretty consistent lately. I mean, ever since I moved into this new apartment—the one with the terrible ventilation and that loud fridge I was telling you about. Moving is just such a massive hassle, you know? I had cardboard boxes stacked up everywhere for the first month, and my schedule was completely thrown off because I was trying to unpack after those ten-hour shifts at the arcade, which is just impossible when all you want to do is collapse. 

But once all the boxes were finally broken down and hauled out to the recycling bin, and the apartment move actually settled into a normal routine... I'd say since then, most weeks I have at least one of these late-night episodes. It's usually just that one night a week where I just completely lose the thread and end up eating way, way past what I ever meant to. 

And then, you know, I have to fix it. I have to do something to make up for it, right? So, like I said, sometimes I'll go down that narrow hallway to the bathroom and try to make up for it by throwing up. But if I don't do that, I still have to compensate somehow. So sometimes I'll just completely skip breakfast the next day. I'll wake up and just drink black coffee—I have this cheap little drip maker on the counter that takes absolutely forever to brew, but it does the job—and I'll force myself not to eat a single thing until much later in the day, even if my stomach is growling while I'm fixing the ticket machines at work. Or, if I don't skip breakfast, I'll force myself to go on a really long run. Which is awful, honestly, because my knees aren't great now that I'm forty, and running on the concrete sidewalks around my complex is just brutal on my joints, but I just feel this intense, overwhelming need to burn it all off. So yeah, at least once a week, it's the eating, and then either the throwing up, skipping breakfast, or just pounding the pavement for miles to try and undo it all.

Well, the throwing up specifically... I guess I don't do that every single time. It really depends on how the night goes and how I'm feeling about what I just ate. Just really, really baffled by the sheer volume of it all and how I didn't even realize I was doing it until it was over.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during these episodes after you get home from work?\n\nPatient: Control? Man, no. Not at all. That's actually the part that really messes with my head the most. Because, you know, at work, I'm totally in control. I have to be. I've got, you know, hundreds of kids and teenagers running around the arcade, the laser tag vests need to be charged, the prize counter has to be restocked, the ticket machines jam up, and I'm the one managing all of that. I'm the guy making the calls and keeping the chaos in check. But then I get home, and it's like... I don't even know. It's like I'm a completely different person. \n\nOnce I start eating on those nights, it’s honestly like I’m watching myself from the outside. Like I'm hovering somewhere up near the ceiling fan—which, by the way, I always keep on medium because my apartment gets incredibly stuffy at night, the ventilation in that building is just terrible—and I'm just looking down at myself on the couch. And in my head, my internal monologue is going a mile a minute. I'm literally telling myself to put the food away. I'm thinking, \"Okay, that's enough, you finished the takeout, you're full, just close the cookie sleeve. Roll the bag up and put a clip on it.\" I even have these heavy-duty plastic chip clips, the magnetic ones that stick to the fridge, they're right there in the drawer next to the sink, it would take two seconds to get up and use one. \n\nBut my hands... it's like my hands don't even belong to my brain anymore. They just keep going. They just keep opening containers, ripping into the plastic wrappers, reaching back into the bags, over and over again until everything is gone. Every last crumb. And I'm just sitting there, completely disconnected from my own body, unable to stop my own hands from moving. It's so bizarre because I know I'm doing it, and I'm telling myself to stop, but the physical action just keeps happening anyway. So, yeah, any sense of control is just completely out the window once that switch flips.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or stressed while you're eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: Anxious? Stressed? Uh... no, not really. It's not like that. I mean, I know people talk about \"stress eating,\" like when you have a terrible day at work and you just want to eat a pint of ice cream to feel better. But for me, it's not like I'm sitting there feeling wound up or panicked while it's happening. \n\nHonestly, it's almost the opposite. Like I said, I'm usually coming off a ten-hour shift. By the time I get home, I am just completely physically exhausted. My feet ache, my back aches, my head is usually throbbing from all the flashing lights and the constant noise of the arcade machines and the music they play on a loop over the PA system—it's this playlist of top 40 hits that just repeats every three hours, and by the end of the week, I feel like I'm losing my mind listening to it. So when I finally get through the door of my apartment, drop my keys in the little ceramic bowl by the door, and kick my shoes off, I'm not feeling stressed. I'm just tired. \n\nAnd then, when the eating starts... like I was describing, it's just this weird, disconnected feeling. I'm not sitting there crying or worrying about my bills or stressing about work the next day. I'm just kind of... blank. It's like my brain just shuts off, or at least the part of my brain that feels emotions just goes offline for a bit. I'm just watching my hands move, watching myself eat all this food, and I'm not really feeling anything at all in the moment. It's just a mechanical process. Grab the food, open the wrapper, eat it, grab the next thing. So no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious or stressed during it. It's more like I'm just running on autopilot, completely numb to whatever else is going on in my head.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Yeah, um... sometimes I do. It's just... well, because like I was saying before about how incredibly full and stretched out my stomach gets, it's just this heavy, rock-solid feeling. And I'll be sitting there on that leather sectional, and the apartment is totally quiet by that point except for the hum of the refrigerator—it's an older model, so the compressor is actually pretty loud when it kicks on in the middle of the night—and I just start thinking about all that food. All those empty takeout containers and the sleeves of snacks and whatever else I just ate. \n\nAnd I just... I can't stand the thought of it just sitting in there. You know? Like, my metabolism definitely isn't what it used to be now that I'm forty. I'm on my feet all day at the arcade, sure, but I just know that if I let all that grease and sugar just sit in my stomach overnight while I'm sleeping, it's going to absorb right into me and turn straight into weight. I can almost picture it happening, just sitting there digesting and turning into fat while I'm just lying in bed. \n\nSo, yeah, sometimes after I get home and eat way too much of that takeout or all those snacks, I'll finally force myself up off the couch and go down the hall to the bathroom. It's a really narrow hallway, and the bathroom is right at the end, and the fluorescent light above the mirror in there is super bright, which is honestly awful at 3 AM when your eyes are already tired. But I'll go in there, and I'll lift the lid, and I'll just... make myself throw up. Just to get it out of me. Because if I can just empty it out and flush it away, then I don't have to worry about it sitting in me and turning into all this extra weight. It's just a way to kind of undo the physical damage of it all, I guess.\n\nDoctor: How often do these episodes of eating a large amount of food happen?\n\nPatient: How often... well, if I really sit down and think about the timeline, it's been pretty consistent lately. I'll wake up and just drink black coffee—I have this cheap little drip maker on the counter that takes absolutely forever to brew, but it does the job—and I'll force myself not to eat a single thing until much later in the day, even if my stomach is growling while I'm fixing the ticket machines at work. Or, if I don't skip breakfast, I'll force myself to go on a really long run. Which is awful, honestly, because my knees aren't great now that I'm forty, and running on the concrete sidewalks around my complex is just brutal on my joints, but I just feel this intense, overwhelming need to burn it all off. So yeah, at least once a week, it's the eating, and then either the throwing up, skipping breakfast, or just pounding the pavement for miles to try and undo it all.\n\nDoctor: How often do you make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Well, the throwing up specifically... So on those nights, maybe two or three times a month, I'll end up in that bright bathroom doing it. But it's definitely not every single time I overeat. It's just when the panic about it absorbing into my body gets too loud to ignore, you know?\n\nDoctor: Do you make yourself vomit after these episodes more often than you initially thought, or has it been consistently a couple of times a month?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's pretty much been consistently a couple of times a month. Like I'm hovering somewhere up near the ceiling fan—which, by the way, I always keep on medium because my apartment gets incredibly stuffy at night, the ventilation in that building is just terrible—and I'm just looking down at myself on the couch. And in my head, my internal monologue is going a mile a minute. I'm literally telling myself to put the food away. I'm thinking, \"Okay, that's enough, you finished the takeout, you're full, just close the cookie sleeve. Roll the bag up and put a clip on it.\" I even have these heavy-duty plastic chip clips, the magnetic ones that stick to the fridge, they're right there in the drawer next to the sink, it would take two seconds to get up and use one. \n\nBut my hands... it's like my hands don't even belong to my brain anymore. They just keep going. They just keep opening containers, ripping into the plastic wrappers, reaching back into the bags, over and over again until everything is gone. Every last crumb. And I'm just sitting there, completely disconnected from my own body, unable to stop my own hands from moving. It's so bizarre because I know I'm doing it, and I'm telling myself to stop, but the physical action just keeps happening anyway. So, yeah, any sense of control is just completely out the window once that switch flips.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or stressed while you're eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: Anxious? Stressed? Uh... no, not really. It's not like that. I mean, I know people talk about \"stress eating,\" like when you have a terrible day at work and you just want to eat a pint of ice cream to feel better. But for me, it's not like I'm sitting there feeling wound up or panicked while it's happening. \n\nHonestly, it's almost the opposite. Like I said, I'm usually coming off a ten-hour shift. By the time I get home, I am just completely physically exhausted. My feet ache, my back aches, my head is usually throbbing from all the flashing lights and the constant noise of the arcade machines and the music they play on a loop over the PA system—it's this playlist of top 40 hits that just repeats every three hours, and by the end of the week, I feel like I'm losing my mind listening to it. So when I finally get through the door of my apartment, drop my keys in the little ceramic bowl by the door, and kick my shoes off, I'm not feeling stressed. I'm just tired. \n\nAnd then, when the eating starts... like I was describing, it's just this weird, disconnected feeling. I'm not sitting there crying or worrying about my bills or stressing about work the next day. I'm just kind of... blank. It's like my brain just shuts off, or at least the part of my brain that feels emotions just goes offline for a bit. I'm just watching my hands move, watching myself eat all this food, and I'm not really feeling anything at all in the moment. It's just a mechanical process. Grab the food, open the wrapper, eat it, grab the next thing. So no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious or stressed during it. It's more like I'm just running on autopilot, completely numb to whatever else is going on in my head.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Yeah, um... sometimes I do. It's just... well, because like I was saying before about how incredibly full and stretched out my stomach gets, it's just this heavy, rock-solid feeling. All those empty takeout containers and the sleeves of snacks and whatever else I just ate. \n\nAnd I just... I can't stand the thought of it just sitting in there. You know? I'm just watching my hands move, watching myself eat all this food, and I'm not really feeling anything at all in the moment. It's just a mechanical process. Grab the food, open the wrapper, eat it, grab the next thing. So no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious or stressed during it. It's more like I'm just running on autopilot, completely numb to whatever else is going on in my head.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Yeah, um... sometimes I do. It's just... well, because like I was saying before about how incredibly full and stretched out my stomach gets, it's just this heavy, rock-solid feeling. And I'll be sitting there on that leather sectional, and the apartment is totally quiet by that point except for the hum of the refrigerator—it's an older model, so the compressor is actually pretty loud when it kicks on in the middle of the night—and I just start thinking about all that food. All those empty takeout containers and the sleeves of snacks and whatever else I just ate. \n\nAnd I just... I can't stand the thought of it just sitting in there. You know? I can almost picture it happening, just sitting there digesting and turning into fat while I'm just lying in bed. \n\nSo, yeah, sometimes after I get home and eat way too much of that takeout or all those snacks, I'll finally force myself up off the couch and go down the hall to the bathroom.
